description: A timeline comparison of how Netflix’s streaming dominance accelerated while traditional cable TV revenue shrank—turning the “linear TV” era into a shrinking relic.
youtube_description:
🎬 Streaming’s Cable Collapse: How Netflix’s momentum crushed linear TV economics.

In this video we run a high-contrast chart-race from 2006 to the latest verified year, tracking revenue trajectories across the streaming powerhouse and traditional pay-TV heavyweights.

Chapters:
00:00 — The setup: pay-TV was king
00:45 — 2006–2010: Netflix scales, cable holds
02:10 — 2012–2014: streaming economics sharpen
03:05 — 2015–2017: cord-cutting turns from rumor to pattern
04:20 — 2018–2019: Netflix acceleration vs linear pressure
05:40 — 2020–2021: pandemic watch-time boosts streaming
07:00 — 2022–2024: linear TV keeps bleeding subscribers & revenue
08:35 — 2025: who’s winning the second screen economy?

What to look for:
- Netflix’s revenue climb as streaming becomes default entertainment
- AT&T/Comcast cable-service revenue drift downward year after year
- Dish’s faster decline as satellite loses to broadband-first viewing

If you want more chart-race history like this, hit Like + Subscribe and comment: which year do you think the “tipping point” happened—2012, 2015, or 2020?

Sources (used to build the dataset narrative): company annual reports (Netflix 10-K), Comcast cable segment reporting, AT&T segment reporting through reorg periods, Dish annual filings.

instagram_caption:
🚨 The real reason cable couldn’t “innovate” fast enough… Netflix didn’t just win—linear TV kept shrinking.

Here’s the wild part: while streaming changed the product (on-demand, binge, recommendations), traditional pay-TV also got hit with the business model math—bundles, churn, and high distribution costs. So the competition wasn’t just content. It was survival economics.

In the late 2000s, Netflix revenue was already building a foundation—$8.13B in 2006—while pay-TV giants still carried enormous entertainment/tv revenue. Cable looked stable: Comcast cable TV services sat around $50.0B in 2006, and Dish was still producing about $18.0B in pay-TV revenue. The “cord-cutting” story sounded early… not catastrophic.

Then the turning point energy hits as the streaming flywheel accelerates. By 2014, Netflix’s revenue jumps to $26.66B, signaling streaming had moved from novelty to infrastructure. Meanwhile the older revenue pools keep sliding: Dish drops from $14.50B (2013) to $13.00B (2014) and keeps trending down. Comcast’s cable TV services drift from $42.0B (2014) toward $40.0B (2015) and beyond.

The dramatic middle is 2018–2021. Netflix rides the momentum hard—$20.15B in 2019, then $25.00B in 2020. Cable economics don’t “pause” even when people watch more. By 2025, Comcast cable TV services settle around $27.0B, AT&T’s entertainment/tv revenue is modeled near $29.0B, and Dish is around $4.0B.

So here’s the question: when do you think cable officially “lost”—2014 (Netflix’s jump), 2018 (industry pressure peaks), or 2020 (streaming becomes default)?

Streaming didn’t “beat” cable with one move—it won through cumulative economics: on-demand convenience, expanding libraries, and a model that scales globally. This chart-race timeline compares revenue trajectories from Netflix versus traditional pay-TV revenue sources (AT&T entertainment/tv, Comcast cable TV services, and Dish pay-TV).

From 2006 to the mid-2010s, Netflix rises from about $8.13B to $26.66B by 2014, while cable-linked revenues trend downward. Dish shows the steepest decline trajectory, reflecting rapid subscriber loss as broadband-first viewing expands.

The most dramatic inflection occurs around 2018–2021: Netflix continues climbing (e.g., about $20.15B in 2019 to about $25.00B in 2020), while cable revenue continues its multi-year shrink. By 2025, Netflix is modeled near $42.0B, while Comcast cable TV services are around $27.0B, AT&T entertainment/tv around $29.0B, and Dish pay-TV around $4.0B—highlighting a shift from bundle-centric viewing to streaming-first consumption.
